title: SKU Rationalization: Process, Metrics and Real Brand Examples | Pattern
summary: What SKU rationalization is, how to run it on Amazon, Walmart and other marketplaces, and how brands reshaped their range with Pattern.
body_markdown:
Product catalogs tend to grow faster than they get pruned. A new flavor here, a bigger pack size there, a color that sold well one season. Each one made sense at the time. A few years later, a brand can be selling dozens of SKUs on several marketplaces, and only some of them are pulling their weight. This steady build-up is often called SKU proliferation.


On marketplaces, every extra SKU carries a cost. It needs stock, a listing, images, ad budget and someone's attention, and it pays storage fees while it waits to sell. SKU rationalization is how brands decide which products deserve that investment.


This guide covers what SKU rationalization is, the marketplace signals to review for each SKU, a step-by-step process, and the options you have beyond cutting a product. It also shows the work in practice. On Tmall, for example, Pattern found that focusing Thorne's Double 11 budget on one or two top-tier SKUs produced more net sales than spreading it across the whole range.


## What is SKU rationalization?


SKU rationalization is the process of reviewing a product catalog to decide which SKUs to keep, modify, consolidate or retire. It's also called product rationalization.


A SKU, or stock keeping unit, is the code a business uses to track each distinct product it sells. Every variation counts separately, so one product in three sizes and two colors is six SKUs.


## SKU rationalization vs product assortment planning


Product assortment is the full range of products a brand offers: how many product lines it carries, and how many versions sit within each line. Assortment planning decides what that range should be, including what to launch and where to sell it.


SKU rationalization reviews the range you already have. Assortment planning sets the range you want to offer. Rationalization checks what you have against it, and what you learn feeds the next plan. We'll come back to how the two work together later in this guide.


## What makes SKU rationalization different on Amazon and other marketplaces


On a marketplace, a SKU is more than a line in your inventory report. It's a listing with its own search rank, reviews, Buy Box and ad history. That changes both what you measure and what it costs to get a decision wrong.


**Fees build up on slow stock.** Marketplace fulfillment programs charge for storage, and slow-moving inventory can attract extra fees the longer it sits. A SKU that looks profitable on a margin report can lose money once those fees are counted.


**The Buy Box decides who gets the sale.** If other sellers offer the same product, most sales go to whoever holds the Buy Box. When a SKU's sales drop, check its Buy Box share first. A lost Buy Box is often a pricing or seller problem you can fix.


**Reviews and rank belong to the listing.** A listing builds up reviews, ratings and sales history over time, and that history helps it rank. Retire a listing and you can lose what it built. Merging near-duplicates into one variation family can keep that value working for the products you keep.


**Ad budget spreads thin.** Every SKU you advertise competes for the same budget. Spreading spend across a long tail of weak products can starve the ones that would grow with more support. Advertising on one product can also lift sales of others, so ad results are part of the decision.


**Weak SKUs affect the brand.** Listings with low ratings, frequent stockouts or high return rates sit next to your best products in search results and on your brand store. Shoppers see the whole range.


## Which metrics should you review for every SKU?


Revenue alone won't tell you whether a SKU is worth its cost. On marketplaces, review each SKU against a fuller set of measures:


- **Contribution margin after marketplace fees,** including referral, fulfillment, storage and advertising costs
- **Sales velocity and sell-through,** and how many weeks of stock you're holding
- **Sessions and conversion rate,** to see whether shoppers find the listing and buy once they arrive
- **Buy Box share,** if other sellers offer the same product
- **Advertising return,** meaning ad spend compared with the sales it drives
- **Ratings, reviews and return rate,** which affect both conversion and the brand
- **Inventory age and storage cost**
- **What it does for the rest of the catalog,** such as bringing new customers to the brand, completing a bundle or carrying the reviews for a variation family


Look at these by channel as well as in total. The same SKU can perform very differently on Amazon, Walmart, TikTok Shop and your own site.


## How to rationalize SKUs, step by step


### 1. Set the goal and the time window


Decide what you're optimizing for. That might be margin, cash tied up in stock, simpler operations, or room to launch new products. Choose a review window long enough to smooth out seasonality, usually at least 12 months of data for established products.


### 2. Pull SKU-level data by channel


Gather the metrics above for every SKU, split by marketplace. Category or brand averages hide the detail you need. A SKU that's weak overall might be strong on one channel and weak on another.


### 3. Sort SKUs into groups


Place each SKU in one of six groups:


- **Grow:** strong performers that would sell more with more stock, content or ad support
- **Fix:** products with real demand that are held back by a weak listing, price, Buy Box or stock problem
- **Watch:** new launches and seasonal products without enough history to judge yet. Set a date to review them, such as after their next peak season.
- **Consolidate:** near-duplicates that would work better as one variation family or a bundle
- **Move:** products that underperform on one channel but could work on another
- **Retire:** products that perform poorly on every measure and do nothing for the rest of the catalog


A common rule of thumb says a small share of SKUs drives most of the sales, often described as the 80/20 rule. Use it as a prompt to check your own data. Your catalog may look quite different.


### 4. Check the halo and dependencies before you cut


Some SKUs matter more than their own sales suggest. A product might bring new shoppers to the brand, appear in bundles, or carry the reviews for a variation family. Advertising on one product can also lift sales of others, an effect known as the[halo effect](https://www.pattern.com/blog/the-halo-effect) . Halo sales are hard to measure precisely, as we explain in our guide to[Amazon brand halo sales](https://www.pattern.com/blog/amazon-brand-halo-sales-advertising) , so check for these links before you retire anything.


### 5. Choose an action for each group


Turn each group into a plan with an owner and a date. For SKUs you're retiring, decide what happens to the remaining stock and the listing.


### 6. Execute in phases and track the results


Make changes in stages, starting with the clearest decisions. Track total sales, margin, conversion and ad efficiency for the range as you go, so you can see whether demand shifts to the products you kept.


### 7. Repeat on a schedule


Demand, competition and costs change, so make this a routine. A quick monthly check on stock age, ad return and Buy Box share catches problems early. A fuller review every quarter keeps the range in shape. Schedule one straight after your biggest sales period, such as January after the holiday season, while the results are fresh.


## What SKU rationalization looks like in practice


Assortment planning sets the range you want to offer. SKU rationalization checks the range you have against it. What you learn from one feeds the next, so the two work as a cycle. Here's how that cycle has played out for brands Pattern works with.


**1. Plan the range for each channel.** Start with the products most likely to succeed where you're selling. When[Holland & Barrett expanded on Tmall](https://www.pattern.com/blog/holland-barrett-case-study-grow-on-tmall) in China, Pattern used data insights to identify three new top SKUs for that market, and the top three now sell more than 4,000 units a month. Sometimes the plan means adding products.[Pura](https://www.pattern.com/case-study/pura) was held back by a limited product assortment on Amazon. After growing its marketplace presence with Pattern, it increased sales 185% year over year in 2024.


**2. Sell, then measure every SKU.** A plan is a starting point. On Tmall, Pattern first promoted Thorne's full range, then tested results for several months before deciding where to focus.


**3. Concentrate on the products that perform.** The data showed that concentrating on one or two top-tier SKUs generated more net sales than spreading budget across every product, so Pattern focused[Thorne's Double 11 campaigns](https://www.pattern.com/blog/how-thorne-compounded-sales-growth-for-3-consecutive-years-during-double-11) there. Low sales don't always mean a weak product, though. For Klean, Pattern deliberately put ad spend behind products that weren't top performers, and[nine of Klean's products reached the top five search results](https://www.pattern.com/blog/klean-ranks-1-on-key-search-terms-with-a-pattern-partnership) .


**4. Restructure, then plan again.** Rationalization often reorganizes a range, and sometimes grows it. For[Johnny Slicks](https://www.pattern.com/case-study/johnny-slicks) , Pattern structured variations and bundles while expanding into new categories, and marketplaces grew from 1% to 20% of the brand's revenue. Thorne's range grew too: its Double 11 promotions expanded to three second-tier products, and over the partnership Thorne grew its SKUs with Pattern by roughly 200%.


Then the cycle starts again. As Feetures put it, working with Pattern "made us more efficient with product assortment to drive a stronger return on ad spend."


## What are your options beyond cutting a SKU?


Retiring a product is only one outcome. On marketplaces, a weak SKU often has better options.


**Improve the listing.** If a product has demand but converts poorly, the problem may be the title, images, price or reviews. Our[Amazon listing optimization guide](https://www.pattern.com/blog/amazon-listing-optimization-ecommerce-guide) walks through the fixes.


**Consolidate into a variation family.** Near-identical products can often be grouped as variations of one product, such as sizes or colors. On Amazon, variations can share one detail page, which concentrates traffic and reviews.


**Bundle it.** A slow seller can become part of a bundle with a stronger product, raising order value and moving stock that would otherwise sit.


**Move it to another channel.** A product that struggles on one marketplace may suit another channel's shoppers better.


**Change the price or pack size.** Sometimes a different price point or pack size is all a product needs.


**Retire it cleanly.** If a SKU has no future, plan the exit. Sell through or remove the remaining stock, and update your catalog so the change doesn't leave broken listings or confused shoppers. Keeping catalog data clean across channels makes this easier, as we cover in our guide to[product catalog management.](https://www.pattern.com/blog/product-catalog-management-a-guide-for-marketplace-brands)


## Why decide marketplace by marketplace?


Each marketplace has its own shoppers, price expectations, fees and competition. A single company-wide keep or cut list misses that.


A product that sells slowly on Amazon might do well on Walmart, where the competing products are different. A giftable bundle might suit TikTok Shop better than a search-led marketplace. A premium size might only make sense on your own site. Holland & Barrett's Tmall range shows the same idea in practice: the right top sellers for China were found from that market's own data.


## Common SKU rationalization mistakes


- **Cutting on revenue alone,** without looking at margin after fees, conversion, Buy Box share or ad return
- **Ignoring the halo,** and retiring a product that was bringing shoppers to the rest of the brand
- **Deleting listings with strong reviews** when the product could have joined a variation family
- **Judging new launches too early,** before they've had a peak season
- **Treating it as a one-off project,** with no regular review afterwards
- **Leaving other teams out,** so retail, operations and advertising plans don't match the new range

## Frequently asked questions


**What is SKU rationalization?** SKU rationalization is the process of reviewing a product catalog to decide which SKUs to keep, modify, consolidate or retire, based on data such as margin, sales velocity, conversion and customer demand.


**Is product rationalization the same as SKU rationalization?** Yes, the terms are usually used interchangeably. Both describe reviewing a product range to decide what stays, what changes and what goes.


**What is SKU proliferation?** SKU proliferation is the build-up of SKUs over time, as new sizes, colors, packs and channel-specific versions are added faster than old ones are retired. SKU rationalization is how brands bring it back under control.


**What is the 80/20 rule in SKU rationalization?** It's a rule of thumb that a small share of SKUs, around 20%, drives most of the sales, around 80%. It's a useful prompt to check your own data. The real split varies by brand and category.


**How often should brands rationalize SKUs?** Run a quick check every month on stock age, ad return and Buy Box share, and a fuller review every quarter. Many brands also review straight after their biggest sales period, while the results are fresh.


**Can SKU rationalization hurt sales?** It can if it's done on revenue alone. Retiring a product that brought new customers to the brand, or deleting a listing with strong reviews, can cost more than it saves. Checking what each SKU does for the rest of the catalog, and making changes in phases, reduces that risk.
